title: Weigh a rock on a triple beam balance: riders in order, poise slid to zero
instruction: Weigh the granite rock on the triple beam balance: with the empty balance at zero, set the rock on the pan, move the 100 g rider and then the 10 g rider along their notched beams, slide the 0 to 10 g poise until the pointer rests on the zero mark, and take your hands off.
context: The triple beam balance is the weighing most adults did firsthand in school science class, and is still the classroom and home-lab balance: no battery and no display, the answer is read off three beam scales once the pointer rests on zero. The skill is controlling a quantity along a path with feedback from a swinging, damped beam: the heavy rider goes in largest first, one notch at a time, to the last notch that keeps the pointer high (going past it swings the beam the other way and the rider has to come back), then the smooth poise is crept along its beam in small pushes, waiting for the pointer to settle, until it rests on zero. The result is read from the instrument, not from the scene, so replaying a memorised pose does not work on a different rock. One hand can do all of it.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left, z up; arm bases at y +0.305 m and -0.305 m. (1) A fixed OHAUS 750-S0 class triple beam balance (610 g capacity, 0.1 g readability; est USD 190 to 230), dimensions estimated. Base plate 0.120 m (x) by 0.515 m (y), 20 mm thick; its knife edge on a pillar at x 0.270, y -0.200, the beams' axis 0.100 m up. The beam turns about x on the knife edge, stops at +-8 degrees, a spring stands for its centre of gravity under the edge (0.269 N m/rad: it outweighs the parts' own weight above the edge and leaves 0.0337 N m/rad, 0.5 g at the pan per degree, with the rock on the pan) and a damper of 0.045 N m s/rad for the magnetic damper (about 3 s to settle). Empty, with every weight at its zero notch, it hangs at zero. (2) Left of the edge: a flat steel pan, 0.152 m across, plate top 0.145 m up, axis 0.120 m left of the edge (x 0.270, y -0.080), on a stem from the beam's left arm. (3) Right of the edge, three parallel beams 8 mm wide and 10 mm tall at 36 mm pitch, ending 0.270 m from the edge: front x 0.234 the smooth 0 to 10 g beam with its 12 g poise (16 mm long, friction 0.30 N, travels 0 to 0.100 m: 1 g per 10 mm); middle x 0.270 the 0 to 500 g beam, notches every 0.040 m, with the 0.300 kg 100 g rider; rear x 0.306 the 0 to 100 g beam, notches every 0.015 m, with the 0.080 kg 10 g rider. Riders are 26 mm across and 20 mm long, astride their beams, 34 mm tall over the beam axis; a rider is drawn into a notch within 10 mm (5 mm for the 10 g rider) and needs about 2 N to push out. All three start at their zero notches, 0.020 m right of the edge. (4) At the beams' right end a pointer hangs 40 mm under the axis (0.265 m from the edge) in front of a fixed scale post with a red zero mark and a mark for every degree (4.6 mm at the pointer). (5) The rock: a granite specimen (2.7 g/cm3), 62 x 48 x 26 mm with a 40 x 30 x 8 mm cap, 0.2364 kg, lying at x 0.130, y -0.170. To make one: cut or grind a granite sample to about that size and trim it until a reference scale reads 236.4 g (+-0.1 g).
scoring: Read at every step from the beam angle, the three weights' positions, the specimen's pose (taken in the beam's own frame) and both grippers; the last step's score counts. Reading = 100 x (100 g rider's notch) + 10 x (10 g rider's notch) + poise (mm / 10), in grams; the specimen is 236.4 g, so the answer is 200 g, 30 g and 6.4 g (poise at 0.064 m). On the pan: the specimen's centre within 66 mm of the pan's axis and 3 to 45 mm over the plate. Both riders in: the 100 g rider within 4 mm of notch 2 and the 10 g rider within 4 mm of notch 3. At rest: the beam turned 0.5 degree or less over the last 1 s. Released and still: over the last 1 s both finger zones 30 mm or more from the specimen, which moved 5 mm or less. Hands clear: over that second both finger zones 30 mm or more from the beam, riders and poise. Fell: latched if the specimen's lowest point is ever more than 20 mm under the table top. Tiers, highest first, the first that holds sets the score: 1.0: on the pan, both riders in, reading within 0.5 g, pointer within 1 degree of zero (one mark), beam at rest, hands clear. 0.75: on the pan, both riders in, reading within 2 g, pointer within 3 degrees of zero, beam at rest. 0.5: on the pan and both riders in. 0.25: on the pan. 0: fell, not released and still, or not on the pan. A beam driven against its stop scores at most 0.5. Real trial: video of the pointer and the three beam scales; read the riders' notches and the poise against its 0.1 g graduations.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. The beam's self-righting is a spring and its magnetic damping a joint damper (est). The pan is a flat rimless plate, rigid on the beam; a rule stands for its Roberval linkage (a load on the plate turns the beam as if it sat on the pan's axis). The three beams lie side by side at one height (real ones step up). Notch detents are a spring rule: a capped pull-in within a capture distance. Weight masses follow the lever ratio (est). No tare knob: the balance starts at zero.
reset_notes: Set every weight at its zero notch (riders on the first notch next to the pillar, poise at the left end of its beam), the pan empty and the pointer on the red zero mark. Lay the granite specimen on the table at x 0.130, y -0.170 m. The balance stays where it is. Nothing is consumed. Real trial: weigh the specimen on a reference scale (236.4 g +-0.1 g, trim by grinding) and check the empty balance reads zero before each trial.
